itens.resumo: Italian Jesuit priest (1618-1663) who discovered and named the diffraction of light, paving the way for the wave theory, and who, together with his confrere Giovanni Battista Riccioli, made pioneering measurements of gravity and of the lunar relief.
itens.corpo:
Francesco Maria Grimaldi was born in Bologna on April 2, 1618, the son of Paride Grimaldi and Anna Cattani. After his father's death, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1632 and was ordained a priest. He taught humanities and, later, mathematics and astronomy at the Jesuit college in Bologna, devoting himself to experimental research until he died in the same city on December 28, 1663, at the age of 45, after eight days of fever.

His most celebrated contribution is the discovery of the phenomenon of the diffraction of light. In a darkened room, letting a narrow beam of sunlight enter through a small opening and observing the shadows cast on a screen by objects of various shapes, Grimaldi noticed that faint fringes of light appeared inside the shadow zone and, in the illuminated zone, faint fringes of shadow. He concluded that light, on passing through the aperture, did not propagate in a strictly straight line but took the shape of a cone. He himself coined the term "diffraction" and carefully measured the number, intensity and coloration of these fringes.

These observations, published posthumously in 1665 in the work "Physico-mathesis de lumine, coloribus et iride, aliisque annexis" (Bologna, printed by the heir of Vittorio Benacci, at the expense of Girolamo Bernia), were the only book Grimaldi published. In the text, he discussed whether light was a substance or an accident and argued that color was associated with undulations of a subtle fluid. Although the theoretical explanation only came with Thomas Young and Augustin-Jean Fresnel in the early nineteenth century, Grimaldi's work served as a documentary basis for the wave theory — Christiaan Huygens used it as evidence that light was a wave. The book includes a brief funeral eulogy of Grimaldi written by Riccioli.

Besides optics, Grimaldi worked in close collaboration with his confrere Giovanni Battista Riccioli: together they were among the first to obtain accurate measurements of the acceleration of gravity at the Earth's surface and to produce maps of the Moon's relief, naming selenographic features with names that are now established. In his honor, the lunar crater Grimaldi and the asteroid 129743 Grimaldi were given his name. His career illustrates how rigorous observation and priestly ministry were able to coexist in seventeenth-century science.

itens.resumo: Dogmatic constitution of the First Vatican Council, promulgated by Pius IX on April 24, 1870, the only conciliar document of the Catholic Church dedicated specifically to the relationship between faith and reason; it affirms that there can be no real contradiction between faith and reason and recognizes the legitimate freedom of the sciences.
itens.corpo:
Dei Filius is the dogmatic constitution on the Catholic faith of the First Vatican Council, promulgated by Pope Pius IX on April 24, 1870, in Session III of the council. The text defines the Church's doctrine on God the Creator, divine revelation, faith, and the relationship between faith and reason. It is the only conciliar document of the Catholic Church dedicated specifically to the bond between faith and reason, which gives it singular weight among the documents of the Magisterium on science and faith.

The vote on the text holds a revealing episode. In a first vote, held on April 12, 1870, the text was approved with 515 votes in favor (placet) and none against (non placet), but 83 votes were of the type "placet iuxta modum", that is, they approved while asking for revisions, many of them concerning the opening expression of chapter I. In view of these reservations, the text presented for the final vote — and approved unanimously on April 24 — changed the order of the words and added "Apostolica": the formula "Sancta Romana Catholica Ecclesia" became "Sancta Catholica Apostolica Romana Ecclesia" (the Holy Catholic Apostolic Roman Church).

In chapter IV, "On Faith and Reason", the document distinguishes two orders of knowledge, distinct in principle and in object: one is known by natural reason, the other by divine faith; beyond what natural reason can attain, there are mysteries hidden in God that can only be known by revelation. On the possible contradiction between the two fields, it affirms that "faith and reason can never be at odds with one another", since the same God who reveals the mysteries and infuses faith has bestowed the light of reason on the human mind, and "God cannot deny himself, nor can truth ever contradict truth". The text adds that the false appearance of contradiction arises, above all, either from the dogmas of faith being misunderstood and set forth contrary to the mind of the Church, or from fabrications of opinion being taken for verdicts of reason.

Far from condemning the cultivation of the arts and sciences, the constitution declares that the Church not only does not oppose this cultivation, but assists and promotes it in many ways, recognizing that the benefits derived from them for human life, having their origin in "God, the Lord of all knowledge" (1 Sam 2:3), lead to God when well used. The doctrine of chapter IV was incorporated into §159 of the Catechism of the Catholic Church and remains a classic reference of Catholic teaching on faith and science.
